title: GI consultation, new patient with trouble swallowing

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi, Mr. Alvarez? I'm Dr. Okafor, one of the GI doctors here. Come on in, have a seat.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thanks. Raymond's fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Raymond, good. So Dr. Lee sent you over, and her note says something about food getting stuck. Tell me in your own words what's been going on.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, so, um, it started maybe three, four months ago. At first it was just like, steak or chicken, I'd swallow and it felt like it sat right here. *(points to lower chest)* I'd have to drink water to push it down.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Right there behind the breastbone, lower part.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah. And now it's bread too. Last week I had a sandwich and I had to go to the bathroom and bring it back up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Liquids, any trouble with water, coffee?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, liquids are fine. It's just solid stuff.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And has it been getting worse steadily, or does it come and go?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Worse. Definitely worse. I've started cutting everything really small. My wife noticed, she's like, why are you eating like a kid.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: *(laughs)* Fair. Have you lost any weight?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think so. My belt's on a new hole. I was about two-fifteen in the summer. I weighed myself Sunday, I was two-oh-one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So roughly fourteen pounds in a few months, without trying.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Without trying, yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any heartburn? Burning in the chest, sour taste coming up?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've had heartburn for years. Like, twenty years. I take the, um, the purple pill sometimes. Not every day. When it's bad.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Omeprazole, or the one called Nexium?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nexium. The over-the-counter one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how often would you say you take it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe two, three times a week? It used to be more. Actually the heartburn's been less lately, which is weird.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, that's useful. Any pain when you swallow, like a sharp pain as food goes down, versus just the sticking?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not really pain. Just pressure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any vomiting blood, or anything that looked like coffee grounds?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Black or tarry stools?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um. They've been darker? But I started an iron pill, so I figured that's why.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Who started the iron?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Dr. Lee. My blood count was low on the physical.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Yes, I see it. Hemoglobin of 10.9, and the iron studies were low. So she started ferrous sulfate in September. Before the iron, were the stools normal color?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think so. I didn't really look, honestly.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's fine, most people don't. Any change in your bowel habits otherwise, diarrhea, constipation?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A little constipated since the iron.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Common with iron. Have you ever had a colonoscopy?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Once. When I turned fifty. They took out a polyp. They told me come back in five years and, uh, I didn't.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. We'll come back to that. Any trouble with your voice, coughing when you eat, food going down the wrong way?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I quit eight years ago. I smoked about a pack a day for, I don't know, thirty years.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Couple of beers on the weekend. Not much.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any family history of cancer, especially stomach, esophagus, colon?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My dad had colon cancer. He was in his seventies. My uncle had something in his stomach, I don't know exactly what.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Other medical problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Blood pressure. And my cholesterol.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I have lisinopril 20 and atorvastatin 40. Anything else? Aspirin, ibuprofen, Aleve?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I take ibuprofen for my knee. Pretty much every day, honestly. Two in the morning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Two of the 200s?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, that's important, so thank you. Any allergies to medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Penicillin. I got a rash as a kid.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright. Let me take a look at you. *(exam)* Take a deep breath for me. Again. Good. Lie back. Any tenderness when I press here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, that's fine.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, you can sit up. So let me tell you what I'm thinking. Food sticking that's getting worse over a few months, solids first, with weight loss and a low blood count, is something we have to look at directly, and soon. There are a few things that cause it. Long-standing reflux can cause a narrowing, a scar-type ring, which is common and very fixable. Reflux can also cause changes in the lining called Barrett's. And in someone with your history of reflux and smoking, we need to make sure there's no growth in the esophagus. I'm not saying that's what it is, but the pattern means we don't wait on it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. That's, yeah. That's kind of what I was worried about.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's a reasonable worry, and the way to answer it is to look. I'd like to do an upper endoscopy, a camera down the throat, while you're sedated. If I find a narrowing I can often stretch it during the same procedure. And I'll take biopsies of anything that looks off. I want this in the next week or two, not months.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And since you're overdue for your colonoscopy, you have a low blood count from low iron, and your dad had colon cancer, I'd like to do the colonoscopy the same morning. One sedation, both done.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, let's do that. Get it over with.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good. Until then, a few things. I'd like you to stop the ibuprofen. It can irritate the stomach and esophagus and it may be part of why your blood count is low. Tylenol is fine for the knee, up to 3,000 milligrams a day. And I want you on the Nexium every day, 40 milligrams, thirty minutes before breakfast, instead of as needed.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Every day. OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Soft foods, small bites, sit up while you eat. If food gets stuck and doesn't pass, or you can't swallow your own saliva, that's an emergency room visit, not a wait-and-see.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Got it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And keep taking the iron for now. I'll order a repeat blood count and iron panel today so we have a fresh number before the procedure. Any questions for me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: How long's the procedure?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Both together, about forty-five minutes, and you'll be in the building around three hours with prep and recovery. You'll need a driver. The nurse will go over the bowel prep with you on the way out.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. Thanks, doc.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: You're welcome. We'll get answers quickly.

reference_note:
**Patient / MRN / DOB:** Raymond Alvarez (fictional), 58 M

**Date of service:** synthetic. **Referral:** Dr. Lee (PCP), progressive dysphagia and iron deficiency anemia. New patient. In person.

### A. History

**Presenting problem:** 3 to 4 months of progressive solid-food dysphagia, localized to the lower retrosternal area. Began with meat, now includes bread. One episode of regurgitation of a sandwich last week. Liquids pass normally. No odynophagia. Patient has started cutting food into small pieces.

**Alarm features:** Weight loss present (about 215 to 201 lb, ~14 lb, unintentional). Dysphagia present, progressive. Anemia present (Hgb 10.9 g/dL, low iron studies, ferrous sulfate started 2 months ago). Melena uncertain: darker stools since starting iron; baseline color not recalled. No hematemesis. No persistent vomiting. Family history: father with colorectal cancer in his 70s; uncle with gastric malignancy (type unknown).

**GI history and medications:** ~20-year history of heartburn, on OTC esomeprazole 2 to 3 times weekly, with recent decrease in heartburn. Screening colonoscopy at 50 with one polyp removed; 5-year surveillance missed. Daily ibuprofen 400 mg for knee pain. Lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, ferrous sulfate. Allergy: penicillin (childhood rash).

**Family and social:** Former smoker, ~30 pack-years, quit 8 years ago. Alcohol: a few beers on weekends. Family history as above.

### B. Examination and data

**Examination:** Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses.

**Data reviewed and interpreted:** PCP labs reviewed and interpreted: Hgb 10.9 g/dL with low iron studies, consistent with iron deficiency anemia.

### C. Assessment and plan

**Assessment:**
1. Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss and iron deficiency anemia. Differential: peptic stricture from long-standing GERD; Barrett's esophagus; esophageal adenocarcinoma, given GERD, smoking history, age, alarm features and lessening heartburn; Schatzki ring (less likely given weight loss).
2. Iron deficiency anemia, possibly from NSAID-related mucosal injury, upper GI lesion, or colonic source. Overdue polyp surveillance and first-degree family history of CRC.

**Plan:**
- EGD with biopsies and dilation if indicated, within 1 to 2 weeks. Indication: progressive dysphagia with alarm features.
- Colonoscopy same session. Indication: iron deficiency anemia, overdue polyp surveillance, family history of CRC.
- Stop ibuprofen. Acetaminophen up to 3 g/day for knee pain.
- Esomeprazole 40 mg daily, 30 minutes before breakfast.
- Repeat CBC and iron panel today.
- Continue ferrous sulfate.
- Diet: soft foods, small bites, upright while eating.
- Return precautions: food impaction or inability to handle secretions, go to ED.
- Prep instructions given by nursing. Patient needs a driver.

### D. Coding

**Level of service:** New patient. MDM moderate to high (undiagnosed new problem with uncertain prognosis; prescription drug management; decision for procedure with identified risk factors).

### E. Attestation

Synthetic note for teaching. Not signed.

title: Chronic pain initial evaluation, low back pain down the leg

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Ms. Brennan? Hi, I'm Dr. Shah. Thanks for filling out all those forms, I know there were a lot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: There were so many. Hi.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I read through them, but I'd rather hear it from you. What's bringing you in?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My back, and my left leg. It's been, God, almost a year now. I was moving my daughter into her dorm last August, I picked up one of those plastic bins, and I felt something, like a pop, low on the left side. And it never really went away.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And the leg, when did that start?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Couple of weeks after. It goes down the back of my butt, the back of the thigh, and the outside of my calf. Sometimes into the top of my foot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Into the top of the foot, toward the big toe?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, kind of between the big toe and the next one.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And what's worse right now, the back or the leg?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The leg. Definitely. The back is like a four. The leg some days is an eight.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What does the leg pain feel like?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Burning. And electric, like a zap, when I bend over. And there's a numb patch on the side of my calf.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What makes it worse?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sitting. Like, driving more than twenty minutes is awful. Bending. Coughing, actually, if I sneeze it shoots down.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And better?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Lying on my back with my knees up. Walking a little actually helps, as long as it's short.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any weakness in the leg? Tripping, foot slapping, trouble going up on your toes or your heels?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't think so. Maybe I catch my toe sometimes? I'm not sure if that's new.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, I'll check that. I have to ask a couple of important questions. Any trouble controlling your bladder or bowels? Numbness in the groin or the area you'd sit on a saddle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Nothing like that.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Fevers, night sweats, weight loss you can't explain, history of cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good. What have you tried so far?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I did physical therapy, twelve visits I think, in the spring. It helped the back a little. Not the leg. I did ibuprofen, which upsets my stomach. My primary put me on gabapentin, 300 at night, and it makes me really foggy in the morning. And I did a Medrol dose pack, which was great for like five days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any injections?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. That's kind of why I'm here.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Have you been on any opioid medication for this? Tramadol, hydrocodone?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I had some Norco after my C-section years ago. Not for this. I don't want to go that route, honestly. My brother had a problem with pills.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I appreciate you telling me, and I agree, it's not where we'd start. How is this affecting your life? Work, sleep, mood.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm a dental hygienist, so I'm leaning over people all day. I've gone from four days to three. Sleep is bad, I wake up when I roll over. Mood... *(pause)* I've been more down. I'm short with my kids. I used to run, and I can't.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's a lot to be carrying for a year. Have you had thoughts that you'd be better off dead, or of hurting yourself?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. No, nothing like that. Just frustrated.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Thank you. If that ever changes, I want you to tell us. Any other medical problems?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hypothyroid. I take levothyroxine. That's it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Smoking, alcohol, anything else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No smoking. Glass of wine maybe twice a week.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And the MRI, I see you had one in July. Let me pull it up. *(pause)* So, at L4-5 there's a disc bulge pushing to the left, and it's pressing on the L5 nerve root as it comes out. That matches where your leg pain goes really well.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Oh. OK. Nobody actually explained that to me.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Let me examine you and then we'll talk plan. *(exam)* Bend forward as far as is comfortable. OK. Lean back. Does that hurt?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not as much as forward.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Lie back for me. I'm going to lift your left leg straight. Tell me when you feel it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: There. Ow. That's it, that's the zap.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: About 40 degrees. And the right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Just tight. No zap.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Push up against my hand with your big toe. Now the right. *(pause)* Left is a little weaker. Walk on your heels for me. Now your toes. OK. Feel this on the side of your calf? Compare to the right.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's duller on the left.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Reflexes are symmetric. OK, you can sit up.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So, here's what I think. This is a left L5 radiculopathy, a pinched L5 nerve from that disc. The leg pain, the numb patch, the positive leg raise and the mild weakness lifting your big toe all line up with the MRI. The good news is that most of these improve without surgery. The mild weakness is something I want to watch.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Since PT and medication haven't been enough, I'd recommend an epidural steroid injection. For your pattern, a transforaminal injection at left L4-5, done under X-ray. It puts anti-inflammatory medicine right where the nerve is irritated. Many people get good relief, often enough to get back into therapy and strengthen.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Does it hurt?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's mostly pressure. We numb the skin. It takes about fifteen minutes. Risks are low but real: a temporary flare in pain, infection, bleeding, and rare nerve injury. Steroids can bump your blood sugar for a few days. I'll give you the written consent to read.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. I'd like to try it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: For the gabapentin fogginess, let's try something different. Instead of 300 at night all at once, we can switch to duloxetine. It helps nerve pain, and it can help mood too. 30 milligrams in the morning for a week, and if you tolerate it, we go to 60.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Is that an antidepressant?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It is, but here we're using it for nerve pain. It's one of the better-studied options for that. Taper the gabapentin over a week as you start it. And I'd like you back in PT after the injection, with a focus on core and nerve-glide work.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Call us right away if you lose bladder or bowel control, get numb in the groin, or the foot gets clearly weaker, like you can't lift it. That's same-day.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Got it. Thank you. Really, this is the first time it's made sense.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm glad. We'll get you scheduled.

reference_note:
**Patient:** Colleen Brennan (fictional), 46 F. Referred by PCP. New patient.

**Chief complaint:** Left low back and left leg pain, ~12 months.

**History of present illness:** Onset ~12 months ago after lifting a storage bin, felt a pop in the left low back. Left leg pain began ~2 weeks later, radiating to the posterior buttock, posterior thigh, lateral calf and dorsum of foot (first web space). Leg pain worse than back pain. Pain scores: back 4/10, leg up to 8/10. Quality: burning, electric with bending. Numbness lateral left calf. Worse with sitting (>20 min driving), bending, coughing, sneezing. Better supine with knees flexed and with short walks. Possible occasional toe catching.

**Red flags:** Denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, history of malignancy.

**Prior treatment:** PT ×12 visits (spring), partial back relief, no leg relief. Ibuprofen, GI upset. Gabapentin 300 mg qhs, morning sedation. Methylprednisolone dose pack, ~5 days of relief. No interventional procedures.

**Opioid history and risk:** No opioid therapy for this condition. Remote post-cesarean hydrocodone. Family history of opioid use disorder (brother). Patient declines opioids.

**Function and mood:** Dental hygienist, reduced from 4 to 3 days/week. Sleep disrupted. Low mood, irritability, stopped running. Denies suicidal ideation.

**PMH:** Hypothyroidism. **Medications:** Levothyroxine, gabapentin 300 mg qhs. **Social:** Non-smoker. Alcohol ~2 glasses wine/week.

**Imaging:** MRI lumbar spine (recent), reviewed and interpreted: L4-5 left paracentral disc protrusion with left L5 nerve root impingement.

**Examination:** Lumbar flexion reproduces leg pain; extension better tolerated. Straight leg raise positive on the left at ~40°, negative on the right. EHL strength 4+/5 left, 5/5 right. Heel and toe walk intact. Decreased light touch lateral left calf. Reflexes symmetric.

**Assessment:** Left L5 lumbar radiculopathy secondary to L4-5 disc protrusion, concordant with MRI. Mild EHL weakness. Chronic pain with functional and mood impact. Failed conservative care (PT, NSAID, gabapentinoid, oral steroid).

**Plan:**
1. Left L4-5 transforaminal epidural steroid injection under fluoroscopy. Risks, benefits and alternatives discussed; written consent provided.
2. Start duloxetine 30 mg qAM ×1 week, then 60 mg if tolerated. Taper gabapentin over 1 week.
3. Resume PT after injection: core stabilization and neural mobilization.
4. No opioid therapy.
5. Return precautions: bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, progressive foot weakness, call same day.
6. Follow-up 2 to 3 weeks after injection; re-check EHL strength.

Synthetic note for teaching. Not signed.

title: Well-woman annual exam with heavy periods
visit_type: Established patient, preventive visit plus problem, in person

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi Priya, good to see you again. It's been about a year.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi! Yeah, right on schedule for once.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: *(laughs)* I'll take it. So this is your annual, but before we go through the checklist, anything on your mind you want to make sure we get to?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Actually, yes. My periods have gotten really heavy. Like, the last six months or so.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, let's start there then. Tell me what heavy looks like for you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So the first two days I'm changing a super tampon and a pad every hour, hour and a half. I've bled through onto the sheets twice. I've had clots, like, the size of a quarter.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: How many days does the period last now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Seven, sometimes eight. It used to be five.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how far apart are they? Still regular?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Regular. Every 27, 28 days. I track it on my app.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any bleeding between periods, or after sex?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Pain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Cramping is worse than it used to be. The first two days I take Advil, like 600, a few times a day.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you feel tired, short of breath going up stairs, lightheaded?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm exhausted. But I have two kids and a job, so I just figured, you know.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Fair, but it could also be your blood count. Any cravings for ice? Some people with low iron start chewing ice.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: *(pause)* Oh my God. Yes. I've been chewing ice all summer. I thought that was just a weird habit.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It's a real clue. We'll check. Are you sexually active, and what are you using for contraception?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, with my husband. He had a vasectomy two years ago.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Any chance of pregnancy otherwise?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any hot flashes, night sweats, changes in mood around your cycle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not hot flashes. Maybe more irritable the week before.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Let's go through the rest quickly. Any new medical problems this year? Surgeries, hospital visits?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Same as always. Just the migraines, which are actually better.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Still with aura?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I get the zigzag lines first. Maybe once every two months now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good to know, that matters for some treatment choices. Medications still just sumatriptan as needed?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: And a multivitamin.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Family history, anything new? Breast, ovarian, colon cancer?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My mom was diagnosed with breast cancer in March. She's 68. They caught it early, she had a lumpectomy.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that. How is she doing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Good. She's doing radiation now. She's tough.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: I'm glad. We'll talk about what that means for your screening. Smoking, vaping, alcohol?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No smoking. Wine, maybe three glasses a week.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Exercise?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I walk the dog. That's about it these days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And how's your mood been overall? Feeling down or hopeless, or losing interest in things?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Honestly, OK. Stressed with my mom. But OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Do you feel safe at home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Your last Pap was three years ago, with HPV testing, both normal. So you're due for that today. Last mammogram was last November, normal. Let me examine you, and then we'll put it all together.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: *(exam)* Breasts, no lumps, no skin changes, no nipple discharge. No lymph nodes under the arms. Now the pelvic exam. You'll feel the speculum. *(pause)* Cervix looks healthy. I'm taking the Pap and HPV sample now. And now I'm going to feel the uterus and ovaries. Uterus feels mildly enlarged, a little irregular on the right side. Ovaries feel normal. OK, all done.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Irregular?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: A little bumpy, which most often means a fibroid. Fibroids are very common at your age and are a classic cause of heavier periods. They're benign. I'd like an ultrasound to see the size and where they sit, because that changes what we'd recommend.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: So here's the plan. Labs today: a blood count, iron and ferritin, and thyroid, because thyroid can also change periods. A pelvic ultrasound. If your iron is low, I'll start iron, and if it's really low we can do an iron infusion, which works faster.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: For the bleeding itself, there are good options, and the ultrasound will help us choose. One option is tranexamic acid, a pill you take only on the heavy days. It can cut the bleeding a lot. Another is a hormonal IUD, which thins the lining and many people end up with very light periods or none. Because of your migraines with aura, I would avoid the combined estrogen pill. The IUD is fine for you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've thought about the IUD. My sister has one and loves it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's a great option for you. Let's get the ultrasound first and decide together. Now, about your mom. With one first-degree relative diagnosed at 68, I'll calculate your lifetime risk, and I'd like to refer you to genetic counseling to see if testing makes sense. Either way, keep yearly mammograms. Your next one is due this month.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. I'll schedule it.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Vaccines: you're due for a tetanus booster this year, and a flu shot. We can do both today.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any questions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, that was a lot but it makes sense. I can't believe the ice thing.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: *(laughs)* It's a classic. I'll message you with the labs.

reference_note:
**Patient:** Priya Raman (fictional), 42 F, G2P2. Established patient. Preventive visit with a separately documented problem.

**Interval history:** No new diagnoses, surgeries or hospitalizations. Migraine with aura, frequency decreased to ~1 every 2 months.

**Menstrual history:** Cycles regular, 27 to 28 days. Over ~6 months: duration increased from 5 to 7-8 days; heavy flow first 2 days (super tampon plus pad every 1 to 1.5 h), nocturnal soaking ×2, clots ~2.5 cm. Increased dysmenorrhea, ibuprofen 600 mg several times daily on days 1 to 2. No intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding. Fatigue and pagophagia (ice craving) over the summer. Mild premenstrual irritability. No vasomotor symptoms.

**Sexual and contraceptive history:** Monogamous with husband, partner vasectomy 2 years ago. Pregnancy not suspected.

**Medications:** Sumatriptan PRN, multivitamin.

**Family history:** Mother, breast cancer diagnosed at 68 (this year), lumpectomy, undergoing radiation.

**Social:** Non-smoker. Alcohol ~3 drinks/week. Walks dog. Mood stable, stress related to mother's illness. Feels safe at home.

**Screening history:** Pap with HPV co-test 3 years ago, normal. Mammogram 12 months ago, normal.

**Examination:** Breasts symmetric, no masses, skin changes or nipple discharge; no axillary lymphadenopathy. External genitalia normal. Cervix normal in appearance; Pap/HPV obtained. Bimanual: uterus mildly enlarged with irregular right contour, non-tender. Adnexa normal.

**Assessment:**
1. Annual well-woman exam.
2. Heavy menstrual bleeding with enlarged irregular uterus, suspected leiomyoma.
3. Suspected iron deficiency (fatigue, pagophagia, heavy menses).
4. Migraine with aura: estrogen-containing contraception contraindicated.
5. Family history of breast cancer, first-degree relative.

**Plan:**
- Pap and HPV co-test collected.
- CBC, ferritin, iron panel, TSH.
- Pelvic ultrasound (transabdominal and transvaginal).
- If iron deficient: oral iron vs IV iron depending on severity.
- Heavy bleeding options discussed: tranexamic acid on heavy days; levonorgestrel IUD (patient interested). Avoid combined hormonal contraception given migraine with aura. Decision after ultrasound.
- Lifetime breast cancer risk calculation; referral to genetic counseling. Annual mammogram, due now; patient to schedule.
- Tdap and influenza vaccines administered today.
- Results via patient portal; follow-up after ultrasound.

title: Behavioral health telehealth follow-up, depression and anxiety
visit_type: Established patient, video visit, medication management

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Hi Marcus, can you hear me OK?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, you're a little frozen. Oh, there you go.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good. Before we start, can you confirm where you are right now? Just the city and state.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm at home. Columbus, Ohio.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And are you somewhere private where you can talk freely?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I'm in my car in the driveway actually. My roommate's home.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That works. And if we get cut off, I'll call you back at the number ending in 4417. Is that still right?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Great. So it's been about six weeks since we bumped your sertraline up to 100. How have things been?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Better. Like, noticeably. Not perfect. But better.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Tell me what better looks like.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm getting out of bed for work without the, like, forty-five minutes of staring at the ceiling. I went to my cousin's birthday thing, which a couple of months ago I would've bailed on. I'm cooking again a little.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That's real progress. What's not perfect?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The anxiety's still there. Like, Sunday nights I get this dread about the work week. My chest gets tight. And I'm still not sleeping great. I fall asleep fine but I wake up at like 3:30 and my brain just starts going.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: What does your brain go to at 3:30?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Work stuff mostly. Did I send that email, is my manager annoyed with me. Money. Just, everything.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: How many nights a week?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Four, maybe five.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any side effects from the higher dose? Stomach upset, headaches, feeling jittery, any sexual side effects?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Stomach was weird the first week. That went away. The, um, the sexual thing, a little. It takes longer. It's not a deal-breaker.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Thanks for telling me, a lot of people don't bring that up. If it becomes a problem, there are things we can do, so let me know. You filled out the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 before the visit. Your PHQ-9 was 9 today, down from 17 when we started. And the GAD-7 was 12, down from 15.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Huh. OK. That tracks.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: On the PHQ-9 you answered "not at all" for the last question, about thoughts of being better off dead or hurting yourself. I still like to ask directly. Any of those thoughts since we last talked?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No. Not this time. That was a dark stretch back in the spring, but no.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'm really glad. And the plan we made back then, you still have the 988 number saved?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it's in my phone.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good. How about alcohol? Last time we talked about cutting back.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm down to weekends. Like, three or four beers on a Saturday. I stopped drinking alone on weeknights.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That's a big change. Has that affected sleep at all?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Weekends I sleep worse, actually. Now that you say that.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Alcohol tends to cause that early-morning waking. Something to notice. Are you still seeing the therapist?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've done four sessions with her. She's doing the, um, CBT stuff. Writing down the thoughts. It's helping with the Sunday thing a bit.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good. So here's what I'm thinking. The depression is clearly responding, and I don't want to rock that. The anxiety and the sleep are lagging behind a bit, which is common, anxiety often takes longer. Sertraline can still go up, but you're six weeks in at 100 and still improving, and the side effect is noticeable. So I'd hold at 100 for another six weeks rather than push it now.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. I'd rather not make it worse, the, you know.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Right. For sleep, I'd like to try something non-medication first. There's a specific therapy for insomnia called CBT-I. Your therapist may already do it, so ask her. In the meantime: if you're awake more than about twenty minutes at 3:30, get up, go to another room, do something boring in dim light, and go back when you're sleepy. Same wake time every day, weekends too.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Even weekends?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Even weekends. That's the annoying part. And keep the phone out of the bed. If we try that for a month and it's not budging, we can talk about a medication.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. I can try.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Also, for the Sunday chest tightness, did your therapist teach you the paced breathing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: She did. I forget to do it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Set an alarm for Sunday at 7 pm. Literally a reminder that says "breathe." It sounds silly, but it works.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: *(laughs)* OK.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'll send the sertraline 100 refill to the same pharmacy, the CVS on High Street?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And let's meet again in six weeks, video again. If anything changes before then, especially any thoughts of hurting yourself, call 988 or our office, or go to the ER.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Will do. Thanks.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Take care, Marcus. Nice work these past weeks.

reference_note:
**Visit:** Synchronous audio-video telehealth. Established patient. Medication management follow-up.

**Telehealth elements:** Patient location verified: home (vehicle in driveway), Columbus, Ohio. Clinician licensed in patient's state. Patient confirmed private setting. Backup phone number confirmed. Consent to telehealth on file.

**Patient:** Marcus Hill (fictional), 31 M.

**Subjective:** Six weeks after sertraline increase to 100 mg daily. Reports improved mood, energy and motivation: getting up for work without prolonged delay, attending social events, cooking again. Persistent anticipatory anxiety Sunday evenings with chest tightness. Sleep: normal onset, early-morning awakening ~3:30 am with ruminative worry (work, finances), 4 to 5 nights/week; worse on weekends after alcohol. Side effects: transient GI upset (resolved), mild delayed orgasm, tolerable. Alcohol reduced to weekends only, 3 to 4 beers on Saturday; no longer drinking alone on weeknights. Engaged in CBT with therapist, 4 sessions completed.

**Measures:** PHQ-9: 9 (baseline 17). GAD-7: 12 (baseline 15).

**Risk assessment:** Denies current suicidal ideation, intent or plan (PHQ-9 item 9 = 0; asked directly). History of passive ideation in spring, resolved. Safety plan reviewed; 988 saved in phone. Protective factors: engaged in treatment, social connection, employment. Risk judged low.

**Mental status (via video):** Casually dressed, good eye contact. Speech normal rate and tone. Mood "better." Affect mildly anxious, reactive, appropriate. Thought process linear. No SI/HI. No perceptual disturbances. Insight and judgment good.

**Assessment:**
1. Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate, improving on sertraline.
2. Generalized anxiety disorder, partially responding.
3. Insomnia with early-morning awakening, likely related to anxiety and alcohol.
4. Alcohol use, reduced; continue monitoring.

**Plan:**
- Continue sertraline 100 mg daily; hold dose for 6 weeks given ongoing improvement and mild sexual side effect. Refill sent to pharmacy on file.
- Insomnia: CBT-I principles reviewed (stimulus control, fixed wake time, phone out of bed); ask therapist about CBT-I. Consider medication if no improvement in 4 weeks.
- Paced breathing with Sunday evening reminder.
- Continue CBT with therapist.
- Counseled on alcohol and sleep.
- Crisis plan: 988, office, or ED.
- Follow-up: 6 weeks, video.

**Time:** 12 minutes. Synthetic note for teaching. Not signed.

title: Primary care follow-up, diabetes and blood pressure plus a new knee complaint
visit_type: Established patient, chronic care follow-up, in person

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Hi Mrs. Washington, how are you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hanging in there, Dr. Kim. Hanging in there.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Good. So we're here for your three-month check on the diabetes and blood pressure. Your daughter came with you today?

turns.speaker: daughter
turns.text: Hi. I'm Angela. I just like to come and listen, she doesn't tell me everything.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: *(laughs)* I tell her enough.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Happy to have you, Angela. Let's start with the sugar. Your A1c came back this morning at 7.9. Last time it was 8.6.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It went down?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: It went down. That's a good drop.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I've been walking. Angela got me one of those step counters.

turns.speaker: daughter
turns.text: She does like four thousand a day now. Before it was nothing.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That shows. How are you doing with the metformin?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I take it twice a day with food. My stomach was bad at first, but it's fine now.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: And the Jardiance?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The new one? I take it in the morning. I have to pee more.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That's expected. Any burning when you pee, or itching or yeast infections?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Are you checking your sugars at home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Mornings, mostly. They're like 130, 140. One time it was 190, after Thanksgiving at my sister's.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: *(laughs)* That one's allowed. Any lows? Shaky, sweaty, confused?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. Blood pressure today was 142 over 86. What are you getting at home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Like 135, 138 on top.

turns.speaker: daughter
turns.text: She doesn't always take the amlodipine. She says it makes her ankles swell.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It does make my ankles swell.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, that's important. How often are you skipping it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe half the time. When I'm going out, I don't take it, because my shoes don't fit.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: That makes total sense, and it's a known side effect. Let's fix that rather than have you skip it. Anything else bothering you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My right knee. It's been killing me for a couple of months. Especially on the stairs, and getting up from a chair.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Did you injure it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, it just started.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Any swelling, redness, warmth?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It swells a little at the end of the day. Not red.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Does it lock or give way?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It feels like it might give way, on the stairs. It hasn't.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: What have you taken for it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Aleve. Two in the morning.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Every day?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Most days.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK. I'm glad you told me, because with your kidneys and blood pressure, I'd rather you not take Aleve every day. We'll talk about that. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, numbness in your feet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My feet tingle a little at night. Both of them.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Alright. Let me examine you. *(exam)* Heart sounds good, lungs are clear. Let me look at your feet. Can you feel this? *(monofilament)* Here? Here?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes. Yes. That one, a little less.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, slightly reduced on the bottom of both big toes. Pulses are good. No sores. Now the knee. Bend it for me. *(pause)* There's some crackling when it moves and a little fluid. Tender along the inside of the joint. Ligaments feel stable.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: OK, so let me put it together. The diabetes is moving the right way. A1c 7.9 from 8.6. Our goal for you is around 7, so we're close. I'd like to keep the medicines the same and keep up the walking. We'll recheck in three months.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: The tingling in your feet is likely early nerve changes from diabetes. Keeping sugar down helps. Check your feet every night, wear shoes that fit, and I'm sending you to podiatry for a yearly foot check.

turns.speaker: daughter
turns.text: I can check her feet.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Perfect. For blood pressure, I'm going to stop the amlodipine because of the ankle swelling and switch you to losartan, 50 milligrams once a day. It also protects the kidneys, which is a bonus with diabetes. Your kidney function last time was fine, but there was a little protein in the urine, so this is a good choice. I want blood work in two weeks to check your potassium and kidney numbers after the switch.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK. One pill a day?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: One a day, in the morning with the others.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: For the knee, I think this is arthritis. I'd like an X-ray to confirm. Please stop the Aleve. Instead, try a cream called diclofenac gel. You rub it on the knee up to four times a day. It works locally, so it's much easier on your kidneys. Tylenol is fine too. And I'll send you to physical therapy. Strengthening the thigh muscles really helps knee arthritis.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Do I need surgery?

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Not at this point. If PT and the cream don't help, we can talk about an injection. We'll take it step by step.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Last thing, you're due for your eye exam for diabetes, and you haven't had your pneumonia shot. Can we do the shot today?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Fine. One shot.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: One shot. *(laughs)* Angela, any questions?

turns.speaker: daughter
turns.text: No, that's everything. Thank you for catching the Aleve thing.

turns.speaker: doctor
turns.text: Of course. I'll see you both in three months.

reference_note:
**Patient:** Dorothy Washington (fictional), 63 F. Established patient. Accompanied by daughter (Angela), with patient's permission.

### Subjective
Follow-up of type 2 diabetes and hypertension.
- **Diabetes:** Walking ~4,000 steps/day. Metformin twice daily with food, GI symptoms resolved. Empagliflozin daily, increased urination; denies dysuria, genital itching or yeast infection. Home fasting glucose 130 to 140 mg/dL, one reading of 190 after a holiday meal. No hypoglycemia. Bilateral nocturnal foot tingling.
- **Hypertension:** Home SBP 135 to 138. Taking amlodipine ~50% of days due to ankle swelling.
- **New: right knee pain** × 2 months, no trauma. Worse with stairs and rising from chair. Mild end-of-day swelling, no erythema. Sense of instability on stairs, no locking. Taking naproxen 440 mg most days.
- **Medications:** Metformin, empagliflozin, amlodipine (intermittent), naproxen OTC.

### Objective
- BP 142/86.
- A1c 7.9% (prior 8.6%).
- Cardiac: regular rate and rhythm, no murmur. Lungs: clear.
- Feet: monofilament sensation slightly reduced at plantar first toes bilaterally. Pedal pulses intact. No ulcers.
- Right knee: crepitus, small effusion, medial joint line tenderness, ligaments stable.
- Prior labs: eGFR normal; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio mildly elevated.

### Assessment
1. Type 2 diabetes, improving, not at goal (A1c 7.9%, target ~7%).
2. Early diabetic peripheral neuropathy, bilateral.
3. Hypertension, not at goal; amlodipine-related ankle edema with nonadherence.
4. Moderately increased albuminuria.
5. Right knee pain, likely osteoarthritis.
6. Daily NSAID use with diabetes, hypertension and albuminuria.

### Plan
1. Continue metformin and empagliflozin. Continue walking. Repeat A1c in 3 months.
2. Daily foot checks (daughter to assist); podiatry referral for annual diabetic foot exam.
3. Stop amlodipine. Start losartan 50 mg daily. BMP (potassium, creatinine) in 2 weeks.
4. Stop naproxen. Topical diclofenac gel up to 4 times daily; acetaminophen as needed.
5. Right knee X-ray (weight-bearing). PT referral for quadriceps strengthening. Consider injection if no improvement.
6. Diabetic eye exam referral. Pneumococcal vaccine given today.
7. Follow-up 3 months.
